references.text: The destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah with fire and sulfur from the Lord, which Jesus refers to as a comparison for the judgment on cities that reject the gospel.
Jesus' parallel statement in Matthew where he says it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah on the day of judgment than for the city that does not receive the disciples.
Jesus says it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom on the day of judgment than for Capernaum, which did not repent despite Jesus' mighty works.
The immediate context where Jesus instructs the disciples what to do when a city does not accept them – they are to go out into the streets and say that even the dust will testify against the city.

Jesus continues by saying it will be more bearable for Tyre and Sidon in judgment than for Chorazin and Bethsaida, further explaining the same principle of stricter judgment for those who have received greater revelation.
The Lord tells Abraham about Sodom's great sin and that he will go down to see if they have acted according to the outcry that has reached him – the background for the judgment on Sodom.
The prophet Jeremiah says that Jerusalem's guilt is greater than the sin of Sodom, reflecting Jesus' principle that greater revelation leads to stricter judgment.

Ezekiel says that Sodom did not sin as much as Jerusalem, and that God removed Sodom when he saw it – this reflects the principle Jesus uses that cities with greater privileges face stricter judgment.
Peter uses Sodom and Gomorrah as an example of God's judgment on the ungodly, in line with Jesus' use of Sodom as a measure for judgment.
Judas mentions Sodom and Gomorrah as examples lying there under eternal punishment by fire, emphasizing the seriousness of Jesus' comparison.
